1.79.oldText: I discovered that a student needing shelter can obtain it for a lifetime for no more than he currently pays in annual rent. If my boasting seems excessive, my excuse is that I boast for humanity, not merely myself; my own faults and inconsistencies do not alter my statement’s truth. Despite much cant and hypocrisy—chaff I struggle to separate from my wheat, and regret as much as anyone—I will breathe freely and stretch myself in this matter. It relieves both body and moral nature, and I refuse to become the devil’s advocate through humility. I shall try to speak well of truth. At Cambridge College, simply renting a room a little larger than mine costs thirty dollars yearly, though the corporation built thirty-two together beneath one roof. The student also endures numerous noisy neighbors and possibly a fourth-floor room. I cannot help thinking that if we possessed more genuine wisdom in these respects, we would need less education precisely because we would already have acquired a greater amount of it; and the financial expense of obtaining an education would to a very considerable degree disappear altogether. Conveniences at Cambridge or elsewhere cost the student or another person ten times as much life as proper management by both parties would require. The highest-priced things are never what the student needs most. Tuition, for example, occupies a large place in the term’s bill; the much more valuable education obtained among the most cultivated people of his generation costs nothing. Colleges are generally founded by collecting dollars and cents, then blindly carrying the division of labor to its extreme—a principle always requiring caution. A contractor is brought in to speculate on the undertaking; he hires Irishmen or other workers actually to lay the foundations, while prospective students supposedly prepare themselves for college. Successive generations pay for these oversights. I think it would be _better_ for students, or those hoping to benefit, even to lay the foundations themselves. A student who secures prized leisure and seclusion by systematically avoiding necessary human labor gets an ignoble, unprofitable leisure. He cheats himself of the experience that alone makes it fruitful. “But,” someone says, “you do not mean that students should work with their hands instead of their heads?” Not exactly, though he might think my meaning much the same. They ought not merely _play_ at life or _study_ it while the community pays for this costly game. They should seriously _live_ it from beginning to end. How could young people learn living better than by trying the experiment immediately? Surely it would exercise their minds as much as mathematics. To teach a boy arts and sciences, for example, I would not follow the usual practice of merely sending him near a professor, where everything except the art of living is taught and practiced. There he surveys the world through telescopes and microscopes, never his unaided eye; studies chemistry without learning how bread is made, mechanics without learning how it is earned; discovers Neptune’s new satellites without noticing specks in his own eyes or the vagabond around whom he himself revolves. He contemplates monsters in a drop of vinegar while surrounding monsters devour him. Who would advance further in a month: the boy making a pocketknife from ore he dug and smelted, reading what the task required, or the boy attending metallurgy lectures at the Institute and receiving a Rodgers’ penknife from his father? Which is likelier to cut his fingers?... Imagine my astonishment on leaving college when told I had studied navigation! A single trip down the harbor would have taught me more. Even the _poor_ student learns only _political_ economy; our colleges do not even sincerely profess that economy of living synonymous with philosophy. While reading Adam Smith, Ricardo, and Say, he consequently plunges his father hopelessly into debt.

1.99.oldText: However incidental and therefore uninformative these figures may seem, their completeness gives them some value. I received nothing without accounting for it in some way. The calculation shows that food alone cost me about twenty-seven cents weekly in cash. For nearly two years afterward my diet was unleavened rye and Indian meal, potatoes, rice, very little salt pork, molasses, and salt; I drank water. Living chiefly on rice suited someone so fond of India’s philosophy. To answer habitual faultfinders, I should add that I sometimes dined out, as I always had and hope to have opportunities to do again. Often this disrupted my household arrangements. But since dining out was a constant element, as I have said, it does not affect a comparison of this kind at all.

1.102.oldText: At first I made bread from Indian meal and salt alone, genuine hoe-cakes baked before my outdoor fire on a shingle or on the end of timber cut off while building. They often acquired smoke and a pine flavor. I also tried flour, but eventually found rye mixed with Indian meal the pleasantest and most convenient. In cold weather baking several small loaves in succession amused me considerably; I tended and turned them as carefully as an Egyptian watching hatching eggs. These were true cereal fruits ripening under my care, with a fragrance to my senses like other noble fruits’. I wrapped them in cloth to preserve it as long as possible. I studied the ancient, indispensable craft of breadmaking, consulting whatever authorities I found. My studies began with the first unleavened bread, when people passed from the wildness of nuts and meats to this milder, more refined food. Then I followed the dough’s accidental souring, supposedly the discovery of leavening, and subsequent fermentations, down to “good, sweet, wholesome bread,” the staff of life. Some regard leaven as bread’s soul, the _spiritus_ filling its cellular structure, preserved religiously like the Vestal fire. I suppose a precious bottle brought on the Mayflower began America’s supply, its influence still rising, swelling, and spreading in waves of grain across the country. Faithfully I fetched this seed from the village until one morning I forgot the rules and scalded my yeast. The accident taught me that even yeast was unnecessary: I made discoveries by analysis, not synthesis. Ever since I have happily omitted it, although most housewives earnestly insisted that safe, wholesome bread without yeast was impossible, and elderly people predicted my vital powers would quickly decline. I find it no essential ingredient; after a year without it I remain among the living. I am glad to avoid the petty business of carrying a bottle in my pocket that sometimes popped and discharged its contents to my embarrassment. Leaving it out is simpler and more respectable. Humanity adapts to climates and circumstances better than almost any animal. Nor did I add sal soda or any other acid or alkali. Apparently my bread followed Marcus Porcius Cato’s recipe from about two centuries before Christ: “Panem depsticium sic facito. Manus mortariumque bene lavato. Farinam in mortarium indito, aquæ paulatim addito, subigitoque pulchre. Ubi bene subegeris, defingito, coquitoque sub testu.” I understand this as: “Make kneaded bread this way. Wash your hands and trough thoroughly. Put meal in the trough, gradually add water, and knead thoroughly. Once it is well kneaded, shape it and bake beneath a cover”—in other words, a baking kettle. Not a word of leaven. But I did not always use this staff of life. Once my empty purse kept all bread from my sight for more than a month.

4.13.oldText: While these goods travel up, others travel down. A whizzing sound draws me from my book, and I see a tall pine felled on far northern hills. Having flown across the Green Mountains and the Connecticut, it shoots like an arrow through the township in ten minutes, almost unseen by other eyes. It travels onward.

4.14.oldText:
“It will serve as the mast
Of some great admiral’s ship.”

8.1.oldText: When I stayed late in town, how pleasant it was to launch myself into the night, especially a dark, stormy one. With a sack of rye or Indian meal on my shoulder, I would set sail from some bright village parlor or lecture room toward my snug woodland harbor. Having made everything secure on deck, I withdrew below with a merry crew of thoughts, leaving only my outward self at the helm, or even lashing the helm in place when the sailing was easy. Many a cheerful thought came to me beside the cabin fire “as I sailed.” No weather ever wrecked or seriously troubled me, although I met some fierce storms. Even on an ordinary night, the woods are darker than most people imagine. Often I had to look up at the strip of sky between the trees above the path to find my way. Where no cart track existed, my feet felt out the faint trail I had worn, or my hands touched particular trees whose positions I knew, letting me steer between them. Thus I would always pass between two pines in the middle of the woods, scarcely eighteen inches apart, on the darkest night. Sometimes, arriving home late on a dark, damp night, I could not remember a single step of the journey. My feet had followed the path my eyes could not see while I dreamed and wandered in my thoughts, until raising my hand to lift the latch woke me. I thought perhaps my body could find its own way home if its master abandoned it, just as a hand finds the mouth unaided. Several times, when a visitor stayed into the evening and the night turned dark, I had to lead him to the cart track behind my house and point out his direction, telling him to trust his feet more than his eyes in keeping to it. On one particularly dark night I sent two young men on their way like this after they had been fishing in the pond. They lived about a mile away through the woods and knew the route perfectly well. A day or two later, one told me they had wandered near their own home for most of the night and arrived only toward morning. Several heavy showers had fallen meanwhile; the leaves were drenched, and so were they, right through to their skin. I have heard of many people losing their way even in the village streets when the darkness was, as the saying goes, thick enough to cut with a knife. People from the outskirts who had driven their wagons into town to shop have had to stay overnight. Gentlemen and ladies making a social call have strayed half a mile, feeling the sidewalk only with their feet and failing to notice when they turned. Getting lost in the woods at any time is a surprising, memorable, and valuable experience. Even in daylight, during a snowstorm, you may come onto a familiar road and be unable to tell which direction leads to the village. You know you have traveled it a thousand times, yet recognize nothing; it seems as strange as a road in Siberia. At night, of course, the confusion is infinitely greater. On even our most ordinary walks we unconsciously steer like pilots, using familiar beacons and headlands. If we stray beyond our usual course, we still hold in mind the bearing of some nearby cape. Only when we are utterly lost or turned around do we appreciate Nature’s vastness and strangeness—and in this world, a man need only be turned around once with his eyes shut to lose his way. Every time we wake, whether from sleep or from absorption in thought, we must learn the compass points again. Only after we lose our way—after we lose the world, that is—do we begin to find ourselves, to understand where we stand and how infinitely far our connections extend.

9.12.oldText: The pond gave me a well already dug. For four months each year its water is as cold as it is always pure; then, I think, it equals any water in town, if it is not the best. In winter, water open to the air is colder than springs and wells sheltered from it. On March 6, 1846, pond water that had stood in my room from five the previous afternoon until noon measured 42°. The room had sometimes reached 65° or 70°, partly from sunshine on the roof. Yet the water was still one degree colder than water freshly drawn from one of the village’s coldest wells. That day the Boiling Spring measured 45°, warmest of all I tested, although in summer it is the coldest I know; in summer, too, shallow stagnant surface water does not mix with it. Walden’s depth also keeps it from becoming as warm in summer as most sun-exposed water. In the hottest weather I generally put a pailful in my cellar, where it cooled overnight and stayed cool all day, although I also used a nearby spring. After a week it was as good as when dipped, without any pump flavor. Anyone camping for a summer week beside a pond need only bury a pail of water several feet down in the camp’s shade to dispense with the luxury of ice.

13.5.oldText: The north wind had already started cooling the pond, though its depth required many weeks of steady blowing. When I began lighting evening fires, before plastering the house, the many gaps between the boards made the chimney draw particularly well. Yet I spent happy evenings in that cool, airy room, surrounded by rough brown knotty boards, with bark-covered rafters high above. The house never looked so pleasing after I plastered it, though I had to admit it was more comfortable. Shouldn’t every room people live in be high enough to allow some darkness overhead, where evening shadows can flicker among the rafters? Such shapes please fancy and imagination more than frescoes or the costliest furnishings. I might say I only began truly inhabiting my house when I used it for warmth as well as shelter. I had acquired two old fire-dogs to lift the wood off the hearth. Seeing soot gather at the back of my own chimney did me good, and I stirred the fire with unusual satisfaction and a greater right to do so. My dwelling could barely accommodate an echo, so small was it. But having just one room and distant neighbors made it seem larger. Every attraction of a house was gathered into that room: kitchen, bedroom, parlor, and family room. Whatever pleasure a house offers parent or child, master or servant, I enjoyed it all. Cato says a family’s master (_patremfamilias_) must have in his country villa “cellam oleariam, vinariam, dolia multa, uti lubeat caritatem expectare, et rei, et virtuti, et gloriæ erit,” meaning “an oil and wine cellar, many casks, so that it may be pleasant to expect hard times; it will be for his advantage, and virtue, and glory.” My cellar held a firkin of potatoes and about two quarts of peas containing weevils; my shelf held a little rice, a molasses jug, and a peck each of rye and Indian meal.

14.11.oldText: Today only hollows in the earth mark these homes, with buried cellar stones and sunny grass bearing strawberries, raspberries, thimble-berries, hazel-bushes, and sumachs. A pitch-pine or twisted oak stands in the former chimney corner; perhaps a fragrant black-birch waves over the old doorstep. Sometimes you can see the well’s hollow, once fed by an oozing spring, now dry and tearless grass. Or the last of the family covered it deep under the turf with a flat stone, to be discovered only in some distant future. Covering wells must be such a sorrowful act! It happens as wells of tears open. Like abandoned fox burrows, these old cellar hollows are all that survives where human life once bustled and people debated “fate, free-will, foreknowledge absolute” in one form or dialect after another. All I can discover of their conclusions is that “Cato and Brister pulled wool,” about as enlightening as histories of better-known philosophical schools.

17.0.oldText: Ice-cutters usually hasten a pond’s breakup by opening large areas: wind-stirred water erodes the surrounding ice even in cold weather. Walden did not respond that way that year, however; she soon put on a thick new garment in place of the old. This pond opens later than every other pond in the neighborhood, partly because her water is much deeper and partly because no stream runs through her to melt the ice or wear it away. I have never known her to open during winter, even in ’52–3, which severely tested the ponds. She generally opens around April first, a week or ten days after Flint’s Pond and Fair-Haven. Melting begins on the north side and in the shallows where freezing began. Less affected by brief temperature changes, she marks the season’s real progress better than any nearby water. A few severely cold March days may greatly delay those other ponds’ opening, while Walden’s temperature rises almost without interruption. On March 6th, 1847, a thermometer placed in Walden’s middle read 32°, the freezing point; near shore it read 33°. That same day, in Flint’s Pond’s middle it showed 32½°, but in shallow water a dozen rods offshore, beneath a foot of ice, 36°. That three-and-a-half-degree difference between Flint’s deep and shallow water, together with its large proportion of shallows, explains its much earlier opening. Its shallowest ice was then several inches thinner than its central ice. In midwinter the centre had been warmest, with the thinnest ice. Anyone wading a pond’s shores in summer likewise notices how much warmer water is close to shore, only three or four inches deep, than a little further out, and how much warmer deep water is at the surface than near the bottom. In spring the sun does more than raise air and ground temperatures. Its heat passes through ice a foot or more thick and reflects from the shallow bottom, warming the water and melting the ice underneath while directly melting the upper surface. This makes it uneven and stretches its air bubbles upward and downward until the whole is honeycombed, finally vanishing suddenly in one spring rain. Ice, like wood, has a grain. When a block starts rotting or “combing,” taking on a honeycomb appearance, its air cells always stand at right angles to the former water surface, whatever the block’s position. Above a rock or log close to the surface, the ice is much thinner and often melts entirely through this reflected warmth. I am told that Cambridge’s experiment in freezing water in a shallow wooden pond allowed cold air underneath, exposing both sides, yet sunshine reflected from its bottom more than cancelled that advantage. When warm midwinter rain removes Walden’s snow-ice and leaves hard, dark or transparent ice in the middle, a band of rotten white ice, thicker though it is, remains around shore, a rod or more wide, produced by this reflected heat. As I have also said, bubbles inside the ice act as burning-glasses, melting the ice below.

17.6.oldText: Sometimes, in a single spring day, this sandy eruption or foliage blankets a bank twenty to forty feet high for a quarter-mile along one or both sides. Its sudden emergence makes these sand leaves remarkable. Seeing the lifeless bank on one side—the sun reaches one side first—and on the other this lush growth made within an hour, I feel I have entered the laboratory of the Artist who made the world and me. Here he still works, playing on the bank, scattering fresh designs in a surplus of energy. I seem closer to the globe’s vital organs, for this overflow resembles the leafy mass of an animal’s entrails. Sand itself anticipates the plant leaf. No wonder earth expresses herself outwardly through leaves: inwardly she labors so intensely with the idea. Her atoms already know this law and are pregnant with it. The overhanging leaf can see its prototype below. _Inside_ globe or animal, the form is a moist, thick _lobe_, a word especially fitting liver, lungs, and _leaves_ of fat (?e?ß?, _labor_, _lapsus_, flowing or slipping down, a lapsing; ??ß??, _globus_, lobe, globe; also lap, flap, and many other words). _Outside_ it is a dry, thin _leaf_, just as _f_ and _v_ are pressed, dried forms of _b_. The root letters of _lobe_ are _lb_: the soft mass of _b_—one lobe, or B with two—with liquid _l_ behind, pushing it forward. In globe, _glb_, the throaty _g_ adds the throat’s capacity to the meaning. Birds’ feathers and wings are thinner, drier leaves still. Similarly, the earth’s lumpish grub becomes an airy, fluttering butterfly. The globe itself continually surpasses and transforms itself, taking wings in its orbit. Even ice starts in delicate crystal leaves, as though poured into moulds left by water plants’ fronds on the watery mirror. An entire tree is only one leaf; rivers are larger leaves still, their pulp the earth between them, their axils holding towns and cities like insect eggs.

18.1.oldText: We ought to look more often over our vessel’s stern rail like curious passengers, instead of travelling like dull sailors picking oakum. The globe’s far side is simply where our correspondent lives. Our voyages merely follow great circles, and doctors treat only skin complaints. Someone rushes to Southern Africa to hunt giraffes; surely that cannot be his true quarry. How long would anyone chase giraffes if free to do so? Snipe and woodcock offer fine sport too, yet I trust shooting oneself would be a nobler kind of hunting.

18.20.oldText: How long will we sit on porches practising stale, idle virtues that any real work would render irrelevant? As though one began a day in long-suffering while hiring someone to hoe one’s potatoes, then went out after lunch to practise Christian meekness and charity with goodness aforethought! Consider humanity’s China pride and stagnant self-satisfaction. This generation rather congratulates itself on coming last in an illustrious line. In Boston, London, Paris, and Rome it recalls its ancestry and complacently discusses its progress in art, science, and literature. Behold the Records of the Philosophical Societies, the public Eulogies of _Great Men!_ Good Adam admires his own virtue. “Yes, we have performed great deeds and sung divine songs that will never die”—meaning while _we_ can still remember them. Where are Assyria’s learned societies and great men? What young philosophers and experimenters we are! Not a single reader of mine has yet lived an entire human life. Perhaps these are merely spring months in our race’s lifetime. We may have had the seven-years’ itch, but Concord has yet to see the seventeen-year locust. We know only a thin skin of our globe. Most people have neither dug six feet down nor leaped that far up. We do not know where we are. Besides, nearly half our time we sleep soundly. Yet we consider ourselves wise and have established an order on the surface. Truly we think deeply and aspire high! Standing above an insect crawling among forest-floor pine needles, trying to hide from me, I wonder why it clings to such humble thoughts. Why hide its head from someone who might benefit it and give its race encouraging news? Then I remember the greater Benefactor and Intelligence above me, the human insect.

18.21.oldText: Newness streams into the world without pause, yet we put up with unbelievable dulness. I need only mention the sermons still heard in the most enlightened countries. Words like joy and sorrow become merely a psalm’s refrain, sung through the nose, while our faith stays with the ordinary and mean. We think only our clothes can change. People call the British Empire great and respectable, the United States a first-rate power. We cannot believe that behind each person a tide rises and falls strong enough to float that empire like a wood chip, if he ever admitted it into his mind. Who knows what seventeen-year locust will emerge next? The government of my world was not devised, like Britain’s, in after-dinner talk over wine.

1.0.oldText: When I wrote the following pages—or rather, most of them—I lived alone in the woods, a mile from any neighbor, in a house I had built myself on the shore of Walden Pond in Concord, Massachusetts, and earned my living solely by the labor of my own hands. I lived there for two years and two months. Right now I am once again a sojourner in civilized life.

1.1.oldText: I would not press my own affairs on my readers so insistently if my townspeople had not asked very pointed questions about my way of life—questions some would call rude, though they do not seem rude to me at all. Given the circumstances they were perfectly natural and pertinent. Some asked what I had to eat; whether I felt lonely; whether I was afraid; and the like. Others were curious to know what portion of my income I devoted to charitable purposes; and a few, who had large families, asked how many poor children I supported. I therefore ask those of my readers who feel no particular interest in me to forgive me if I undertake to answer some of these questions in this book. In most books the _I_, or first person, is left out; in this one it will be kept. That, when it comes to egotism, is the main difference. We commonly forget that it is, after all, always the first person who is speaking. I would not talk so much about myself if I knew anyone else as well. Unfortunately, the narrowness of my experience confines me to this subject. Moreover, I for my part demand of every writer, sooner or later, a simple and sincere account of his own life—not merely what he has heard about other men's lives; the kind of account he would send to his relatives from a distant land. For if he has lived sincerely, he must have lived in a land distant from mine. Perhaps these pages are addressed more particularly to poor students. As for the rest of my readers, they will accept whatever portions apply to them. I trust that no one will stretch the seams in putting on the coat, for it may serve well anyone whom it fits.

1.2.oldText: I would gladly say something—not so much about the Chinese and Sandwich Islanders as about you who read these pages, who are said to live in New England; something about your condition, especially your outward condition or circumstances in this world, in this town: what it is, whether it has to be as bad as it is, and whether it cannot be improved as easily as not. I have traveled a good deal in Concord; and everywhere—in shops, offices, and fields—the inhabitants have appeared to me to be doing penance in a thousand remarkable ways. What I have heard of Brahmins sitting exposed to four fires and staring into the face of the sun; or hanging head-downward over flames; or gazing at the heavens over their shoulders “until it becomes impossible for them to resume their natural position, while from the twist of the neck nothing but liquids can pass into the stomach;” or living chained for life at the foot of a tree; or measuring vast empires with their bodies, like caterpillars; or standing on one leg on top of pillars—even these forms of deliberate penance are scarcely more incredible or astonishing than the scenes I witness every day. The twelve labors of Hercules were trifling compared with what my neighbors have undertaken; for those were only twelve, and they had an end. But I could never see that these men killed or captured any monster, or finished any labor. They have no friend Iolas to burn out the root of the hydra's head with a hot iron; as soon as one head is crushed, two spring up.

1.3.oldText: I see young men, my fellow townsmen, whose misfortune is to have inherited farms, houses, barns, cattle, and farming tools—because these are easier to acquire than to get rid of. They would have been better off born in the open pasture and suckled by a wolf, so that they might have seen with clearer eyes what field they were called to labor in. Who made them serfs of the soil? Why should they eat their sixty acres, when man is condemned to eat only his peck of dirt? Why should they begin digging their own graves the moment they are born? They have to live a man's life, pushing all these things in front of them, and get on as best they can. How many a poor immortal soul have I met nearly crushed and smothered beneath its load, creeping down the road of life, pushing before it a barn seventy-five feet by forty, its Augean stables never cleansed, plus one hundred acres of land—tillage, mowing, pasture, and wood-lot! Those without inheritance, who struggle with no such unnecessary encumbrances, find it labor enough to subdue and cultivate a few cubic feet of flesh.

1.4.oldText: But men labor under a mistake. The better part of a man is soon plowed into the soil for compost. By an apparent fate, commonly called necessity, they spend their lives—as an old book puts it—laying up treasures that moth and rust will corrupt and that thieves will break through and steal. It is a fool's life, as they will discover when they reach the end of it, if not sooner. It is said that Deucalion and Pyrrha created humankind by throwing stones over their heads behind them:—

1.5.oldText: Inde genus durum sumus, experiensque laborum, Et documenta damus quâ simus origine nati.

1.6.oldText: Or, as Raleigh rhymes it in his sonorous way,—

1.7.oldText: “From thence our kind hard-hearted is, enduring pain and care, Approving that our bodies of a stony nature are.”

1.8.oldText: So much for blind obedience to a blundering oracle—throwing stones over their heads behind them, and not seeing where they fell.

1.9.oldText: Most men, even in this comparatively free country, through sheer ignorance and error, are so consumed by the artificial cares and needlessly coarse labors of life that they cannot reach for its finer fruits. Their fingers, from constant toil, are too clumsy and too shaky for that. In practice, the laboring man has no leisure for genuine integrity day by day; he cannot afford to maintain the most manly relations with other men; his labor would be devalued in the market. He has no time to be anything but a machine. How can he properly remember his own ignorance—which his growth requires—when he must so often draw on his knowledge? We should sometimes feed and clothe him for free, and revive him with our cordials, before we judge him. The finest qualities of our nature, like the bloom on fruit, can be preserved only by the most delicate handling. Yet we do not treat ourselves, or one another, with that kind of tenderness.

1.10.oldText: Some of you, as we all know, are poor and find it hard to live—are sometimes, as it were, gasping for breath. I have no doubt that some of you reading this book are unable to pay for all the dinners you have actually eaten, or for the coats and shoes that are already wearing out or worn out, and have come to this page to spend borrowed or stolen time, robbing your creditors of an hour. It is very obvious what mean and sneaking lives many of you lead, for my eyes have been sharpened by experience: always on the edge, trying to break into business and trying to get out of debt, a very ancient bog the Latins called _æs alienum_, another's brass—for some of their coins were made of brass; still living, and dying, and being buried by this other man's brass; always promising to pay, promising to pay tomorrow, and dying today insolvent; trying to curry favor and drum up custom by every possible means short of state-prison offenses; lying, flattering, voting, contracting yourselves down into a nutshell of civility or expanding into an atmosphere of thin, vaporous generosity, all so you can persuade your neighbor to let you make his shoes, or his hat, or his coat, or his carriage, or import his groceries for him; making yourselves sick so that you may put something aside against a sick day—something to be tucked away in an old chest, or in a stocking behind the plastering, or, more safely, in the brick bank; no matter where, no matter how much or how little.

1.11.oldText: I sometimes marvel that we can be so frivolous—I might almost say—as to give our attention to the gross but rather foreign form of servitude called Negro Slavery, when there are so many keen and subtle masters enslaving us both north and south. It is hard to have a southern overseer; it is worse to have a northern one; but worst of all is to be the slave-driver of yourself. Talk about divinity in man! Look at the teamster on the highway, hauling his load to market by day or by night; does any divinity stir within him? His highest duty is to feed and water his horses! What is his own destiny to him, compared with the shipping interests? Doesn't he drive for Squire Make-a-stir? How godlike, how immortal, is he? See how he cowers and sneaks, how vaguely he fears all day long—not because he is not immortal or divine, but because he is the slave and prisoner of his own opinion of himself, a reputation won by his own deeds. Public opinion is a weak tyrant compared with our own private opinion. What a man thinks of himself—that is what determines, or rather indicates, his fate. Self-emancipation even in the West Indian provinces of fancy and imagination—what Wilberforce is there to bring that about? Think too of the ladies of the land weaving toilet cushions against the last day, so as not to betray too keen an interest in their own fates! As if you could kill time without injuring eternity.

1.12.oldText: The mass of men lead lives of quiet desperation. What is called resignation is confirmed desperation. From the desperate city you go out into the desperate country, and you have to console yourself with the bravery of minks and muskrats. A stereotyped but unconscious despair lies hidden even beneath what are called the games and amusements of mankind. There is no real play in them, for play comes after work. But it is a mark of wisdom not to do desperate things.

1.13.oldText: When we consider what—to use the words of the catechism—is the chief end of man, and what are the true necessaries and means of life, it appears as if men had deliberately chosen the common mode of living because they preferred it to any other. Yet they honestly believe there is no choice left. But alert and healthy natures remember that the sun rose clear. It is never too late to give up our prejudices. No way of thinking or doing, however ancient, can be trusted without proof. What everyone echoes today, or silently passes by as true, may turn out tomorrow to be falsehood—mere smoke of opinion, which some had trusted for a cloud that would sprinkle fertilizing rain on their fields. What old people say you cannot do, you try and find that you can. Old deeds for old people, and new deeds for new. Old people once did not know enough, perhaps, to fetch fresh fuel to keep the fire going; new people put a little dry wood under a pot and are whirled around the globe with the speed of birds, in a way that, as the phrase goes, kills old people. Age is no better—hardly as well—qualified to be an instructor as youth, for it has not gained as much as it has lost. One may almost doubt whether the wisest man has learned anything of absolute value by living. Practically speaking, the old have no very important advice to give the young; their own experience has been so partial, and their lives have been such miserable failures, for private reasons, as they must believe; and perhaps they have some faith left that belies that experience, and they are only less young than they were. I have lived some thirty years on this planet, and I have yet to hear the first syllable of valuable or even earnest advice from my elders. They have told me nothing, and probably cannot tell me anything to the purpose. Here is life, an experiment to a great extent untried by me; and it does not help me that they have tried it. If I have any experience I consider valuable, I am sure to reflect that my Mentors said nothing about it.

1.14.oldText: One farmer says to me, “You cannot live on vegetable food alone, for it furnishes nothing to make bones with;” and so he religiously devotes part of his day to supplying his system with the raw material of bones; walking all the while he talks behind his oxen, which, with vegetable-made bones, jerk him and his lumbering plow along in spite of every obstacle. Some things are real necessities of life in some circles—the most helpless and diseased—which in others are mere luxuries, and in others still are entirely unknown.

1.15.oldText: The whole ground of human life seems to some to have been gone over by their predecessors—both the heights and the valleys—and everything cared for. According to Evelyn, “the wise Solomon prescribed ordinances for the very distances of trees; and the Roman prætors have decided how often you may go into your neighbor's land to gather the acorns which fall on it without trespass, and what share belongs to that neighbor.” Hippocrates has even left directions on how we should cut our nails: even with the ends of the fingers, neither shorter nor longer. No doubt the very tedium and ennui that claim to have exhausted the variety and the joys of life are as old as Adam. But man's capacities have never been measured; nor are we to judge what he can do by any precedents, so little has been tried. Whatever your failures may have been so far, “be not afflicted, my child, for who shall assign to thee what thou hast left undone?”

1.16.oldText: We might test our lives by a thousand simple checks; for instance, the very same sun that ripens my beans illuminates, at the same moment, a whole system of earths like ours. If I had remembered this, it would have prevented some mistakes. That was not the light by which I hoed them. The stars are the apexes of what wonderful triangles! What distant and different beings, in the various mansions of the universe, are contemplating the same one at the same moment! Nature and human life are as various as our individual constitutions. Who can say what life offers as a prospect to another person? Could any greater miracle take place than for us to look through one another's eyes for an instant? We should live through all the ages of the world in an hour—indeed, through all the worlds of the ages. History, Poetry, Mythology!—I know of no reading of another's experience that would be so startling and informing as this would be.

1.17.oldText: The greater part of what my neighbors call good I believe in my soul to be bad, and if I repent of anything, it is very likely my good behavior. What demon possessed me, that I behaved so well? You may say the wisest thing you can, old man—you who have lived seventy years, and not without a kind of honor—but I hear an irresistible voice calling me away from all that. One generation abandons the enterprises of another like stranded ships.

1.18.oldText: I think we may safely trust a good deal more than we do. We may waive just as much care of ourselves as we honestly bestow elsewhere. Nature is as well adapted to our weakness as to our strength. The incessant anxiety and strain that drives some people is a nearly incurable form of disease. We are made to exaggerate the importance of whatever work we do; and yet how much is not done by us! Or what if we had been taken sick? How vigilant we are! Determined not to live by faith if we can avoid it. On the alert all day long, at night we unwillingly say our prayers and commit ourselves to uncertainties. So thoroughly and sincerely are we compelled to live, revering our life and denying any possibility of change. This is the only way, we say; but there are as many ways as there can be radii drawn from one center. All change is a miracle to contemplate; but it is a miracle taking place every instant. Confucius said, “To know that we know what we know, and that we do not know what we do not know, that is true knowledge.” When one man has reduced a fact of the imagination to a fact for his understanding, I foresee that all men will at last establish their lives on that basis.

1.19.oldText: Let us consider for a moment what most of the trouble and anxiety I have referred to is about, and how much it is necessary that we be troubled, or at least careful. It would be some advantage to live a primitive, frontier life—even in the midst of an outward civilization—if only to learn what the gross necessaries of life are and what methods have been used to obtain them; or even to look over the old day-books of the merchants, to see what people most commonly bought at the stores, what they stocked—that is, what the grossest groceries are. For the improvements of ages have had little influence on the essential laws of human existence; just as our skeletons are probably indistinguishable from those of our ancestors.

1.20.oldText: By the words _necessary of life_ I mean whatever, of all that man obtains by his own exertions, has from the start—or through long use has become—so important to human life that few people, if any, whether from savageness, poverty, or philosophy, ever try to do without it. For many creatures there is in this sense just one necessary of life: Food. For the bison of the prairie it is a few inches of palatable grass and water to drink—unless he seeks the Shelter of the forest or the mountain's shadow. None of the brute creation requires more than Food and Shelter. The necessaries of life for man in this climate may, accurately enough, be sorted under the several headings of Food, Shelter, Clothing, and Fuel; for not until we have secured these are we ready to face the true problems of life with freedom and a prospect of success. Man has invented not only houses but clothes and cooked food; and possibly from the accidental discovery of the warmth of fire, and the use of it that followed—at first a luxury—arose the present necessity of sitting by it. We observe cats and dogs acquiring the same second nature. By proper Shelter and Clothing we legitimately retain our own internal heat; but with an excess of these, or of Fuel—that is, with an external heat greater than our own internal heat—may not cookery properly be said to begin? Darwin, the naturalist, says of the inhabitants of Tierra del Fuego that, while his own party, well clothed and sitting close to a fire, were far from too warm, these naked savages, who were farther off, were observed—to his great surprise—“to be streaming with perspiration at undergoing such a roasting.” We are told likewise that the New Hollander goes naked with impunity, while the European shivers in his clothes. Is it impossible to combine the hardiness of these savages with the intellect of the civilized man? According to Liebig, man's body is a stove, and food is the fuel that keeps up the internal combustion in the lungs. In cold weather we eat more, in warm weather less. Animal heat is the result of a slow combustion, and disease and death occur when it is too rapid; or, for want of fuel or some defect in the draft, the fire goes out. Of course vital heat is not to be confused with fire; but so much for the analogy. It appears, then, from the above list, that the expression _animal life_ is nearly synonymous with the expression _animal heat_; for while Food may be regarded as the Fuel that keeps the fire going inside us—and Fuel serves only to prepare that Food or to increase the warmth of our bodies by adding heat from outside—Shelter and Clothing also serve only to retain the _heat_ thus generated and absorbed.

1.21.oldText: The grand necessity, then, for our bodies is to keep warm—to keep the vital heat in us. What pains we accordingly take, not only with our Food, Clothing, and Shelter, but with our beds, which are our night-clothes, robbing the nests and breasts of birds to prepare this shelter within a shelter, as the mole has its bed of grass and leaves at the end of its burrow! The poor man is apt to complain that this is a cold world; and to cold, no less social than physical, we directly attribute a great part of our ills. In some climates summer makes a kind of Elysian life possible for man. Fuel, except to cook his Food, is then unnecessary; the sun is his fire, and many of the fruits are sufficiently cooked by its rays; meanwhile Food is generally more varied and more easily obtained, and Clothing and Shelter are wholly or half unnecessary. At the present day, and in this country, as I find by my own experience, a few tools—a knife, an axe, a spade, a wheelbarrow, etc.—and for the studious, lamplight, stationery, and access to a few books, rank next to necessaries and can all be obtained at a trifling cost. Yet some, unwisely, go to the other side of the globe, to barbarous and unhealthy regions, and devote themselves to trade for ten or twenty years just so that they may live—that is, keep comfortably warm—and at last die in New England. The luxuriously rich are not merely kept comfortably warm but unnaturally hot; as I implied before, they are cooked, of course _à la mode_.

1.22.oldText: Most of the luxuries, and many of the so-called comforts of life, are not only not indispensable, they are positive hindrances to the elevation of mankind. With respect to luxuries and comforts, the wisest have always lived more simple and meager lives than the poor. The ancient philosophers—Chinese, Hindoo, Persian, and Greek—were a class than which none has been poorer in outward riches, and none so rich in inward. We do not know much about them. It is remarkable that _we_ know as much about them as we do. The same is true of the more modern reformers and benefactors of their race. None can be an impartial or wise observer of human life except from the vantage ground of what we should call voluntary poverty. The fruit of a life of luxury is luxury, whether in agriculture, commerce, literature, or art. Nowadays there are professors of philosophy, but not philosophers. Yet it is admirable to profess because it was once admirable to live. To be a philosopher is not merely to have subtle thoughts, nor even to found a school, but so to love wisdom as to live according to its dictates—a life of simplicity, independence, magnanimity, and trust. It is to solve some of the problems of life, not only theoretically, but practically. The success of great scholars and thinkers is commonly a courtier-like success—not kingly, not manly. They get by merely through conformity, much as their fathers did, and are in no sense the progenitors of a nobler race of men. But why do men degenerate at all? What makes families die out? What is the nature of the luxury that enervates and destroys nations? Are we sure that there is none of it in our own lives? The philosopher is in advance of his age even in the outward form of his life. He is not fed, sheltered, clothed, or warmed like his contemporaries. How can a man be a philosopher and not maintain his vital heat by better methods than other men?

1.23.oldText: When a man is warmed by the several methods I have described, what does he want next? Surely not more warmth of the same kind—more and richer food, larger and more splendid houses, finer and more abundant clothing, more numerous, incessant, and hotter fires, and the like. When he has obtained the things necessary to life, there is another alternative besides accumulating superfluities: to venture out into life now, his vacation from humbler toil having begun. The soil, it appears, is suited to the seed, since it has sent its little root downward; and now it may send its shoot upward too, with confidence. Why has man rooted himself thus firmly in the earth, except so that he may rise in the same proportion into the heavens above?—for the nobler plants are valued for the fruit they at last bear in the air and light, far from the ground, and are not treated like the humbler edibles, which, though they may be biennials, are cultivated only until they have perfected their root, and are often cut down at the top for this purpose, so that most people would not recognize them in their flowering season.

1.24.oldText: I do not mean to prescribe rules to strong and valiant natures, who will mind their own business whether in heaven or hell, and perhaps build more magnificently and spend more lavishly than the richest without ever impoverishing themselves—not knowing how they live, if indeed there are any such people, as has been dreamed; nor to those who find their encouragement and inspiration in precisely the present condition of things, and cherish it with the fondness and enthusiasm of lovers—and, to some extent, I count myself in this number. I am not speaking to those who are well employed in whatever circumstances—they know whether they are well employed or not. I am speaking mainly to the mass of men who are discontented, idly complaining about the hardness of their lot or of the times, when they might be improving them. There are some who complain most energetically and inconsolably, because they are, as they say, doing their duty. I also have in mind that seemingly wealthy but most terribly impoverished class of all—those who have piled up dross but do not know how to use it, or how to get rid of it, and have thus forged their own golden or silver fetters.

1.25.oldText: If I were to try to tell how I have wished to spend my life in years past, it would probably surprise those of my readers who are somewhat acquainted with its actual history; it would certainly astonish those who know nothing about it. I will only hint at some of the enterprises I have cherished.

1.26.oldText: In any weather, at any hour of the day or night, I have been anxious to seize the nick of time, and to notch it on my stick too; to stand on the meeting of two eternities, the past and the future—which is precisely the present moment—and to toe that line. You will forgive some obscurities, for there are more secrets in my trade than in most men's, and yet they are not deliberately kept; they are inseparable from its very nature. I would gladly tell everything I know about it, and never paint “No Admittance” on my gate.

1.27.oldText: I long ago lost a hound, a bay horse, and a turtle-dove, and I am still on their trail. I have spoken with many travelers concerning them, describing their tracks and the calls they answered to. I have met one or two who had heard the hound, and the tramp of the horse, and had even seen the dove disappear behind a cloud, and they seemed as eager to recover them as if they had lost them themselves.

1.28.oldText: To anticipate, not just the sunrise and the dawn, but, if possible, Nature herself! How many mornings, summer and winter, before any neighbor was up and about his business, have I been about mine! No doubt many of my townsmen have met me returning from this enterprise—farmers setting out for Boston in the twilight, or woodchoppers going to their work. It is true I never materially assisted the sun in his rising; but make no mistake, it was of the utmost importance simply to be present at it.

1.29.oldText: So many autumn—yes, and winter—days I spent outside the town, trying to hear what was in the wind, to catch it and carry it express! I nearly sank all my capital in it, and lost my own breath into the bargain, running in the face of it. If it had concerned either of the political parties, you may be sure it would have appeared in the Gazette with the earliest news. At other times I watched from the observatory of some cliff or tree, to telegraph any new arrival; or waited at evening on the hilltops for the sky to fall, so that I might catch something—though I never caught much, and what I did, manna-like, dissolved again in the sun.

1.30.oldText: For a long time I was reporter to a journal of no very wide circulation, whose editor has never yet seen fit to print the bulk of my contributions; and, as is too common with writers, I got only my labor for my pains. However, in this case my pains were their own reward.

1.31.oldText: For many years I was self-appointed inspector of snowstorms and rainstorms, and did my duty faithfully; surveyor, if not of highways, then of forest paths and all cross-lot routes, keeping them open, and ravines bridged and passable in all seasons, wherever the public heel had testified to their usefulness.

1.32.oldText: I have looked after the wild stock of the town, which give a faithful herdsman a good deal of trouble by leaping fences; and I have kept an eye on the unfrequented nooks and corners of the farm—though I did not always know whether Jonas or Solomon was working in a particular field today; that was none of my business. I have watered the red huckleberry, the sand cherry and the nettle tree, the red pine and the black ash, the white grape and the yellow violet, which might otherwise have withered in dry seasons.

1.33.oldText: In short, I went on this way for a long time—I may say it without boasting—faithfully minding my business, until it became more and more obvious that my townsmen were not, after all, going to admit me to the list of town officers, nor make my position a sinecure with a modest stipend. My accounts, which I can swear to have kept faithfully, have indeed never been audited—still less accepted, still less paid and settled. However, I have not set my heart on that.

1.34.oldText: Not long ago, a wandering Indian went to sell baskets at the house of a well-known lawyer in my neighborhood. “Do you wish to buy any baskets?” he asked. “No, we do not want any,” was the reply. “What!” exclaimed the Indian as he went out the gate, “do you mean to starve us?” Having seen his industrious white neighbors so well off—that the lawyer only had to weave arguments, and by some magic wealth and standing followed—he had said to himself: I will go into business; I will weave baskets; it is something I can do. He thought that once he had made the baskets, he would have done his part, and then it would be the white man's job to buy them. He had not realized that he needed to make it worth the other man's while to buy them, or at least to make him think it was, or to make something else that would be worth the other man's while to buy. I too had woven a kind of basket of delicate texture, but I had not made it worth anyone's while to buy them. Yet none the less, in my case, I thought it worth my while to weave them; and instead of studying how to make it worth men's while to buy my baskets, I studied rather how to avoid the necessity of selling them. The life that men praise and regard as successful is but one kind. Why should we exaggerate any one kind at the expense of the others?

1.35.oldText: Finding that my fellow citizens were not likely to offer me any room in the courthouse, or any curacy or living anywhere else, but that I must shift for myself, I turned my face more exclusively than ever to the woods, where I was better known. I determined to go into business at once, and not wait to acquire the usual capital, using whatever slender means I had already gotten. My purpose in going to Walden Pond was not to live cheaply nor to live luxuriously there, but to transact some private business with the fewest obstacles; to be hindered from accomplishing this for want of a little common sense, a little enterprise and business talent, appeared not so sad as foolish.

1.36.oldText: I have always tried to acquire strict business habits; they are indispensable to every man. If your trade is with the Celestial Empire, then some small counting house on the coast, in some Salem harbor, will be fixture enough. You will export such articles as the country affords, purely native products: much ice and pine timber and a little granite, always in native ships. These will be good ventures. To oversee all the details yourself in person; to be at once pilot and captain, and owner and underwriter; to buy and sell and keep the accounts; to read every letter received, and write or read every letter sent; to supervise the discharge of imports night and day; to be on many parts of the coast almost at the same time—often the richest freight will be discharged on a Jersey shore—to be your own telegraph, untiringly sweeping the horizon, hailing all passing vessels bound coastwise; to keep up a steady dispatch of commodities, for the supply of so distant and exorbitant a market; to keep yourself informed of the state of the markets, the prospects of war and peace everywhere, and anticipate the tendencies of trade and civilization—taking advantage of the results of all exploring expeditions, using new passages and all improvements in navigation; charts to be studied, the position of reefs and new lights and buoys to be ascertained, and ever and ever the logarithmic tables to be corrected, for by the error of some calculator the vessel often splits upon a rock that should have reached a friendly pier—there is the untold fate of La Perouse; universal science to be kept pace with, studying the lives of all great discoverers and navigators, great adventurers and merchants, from Hanno and the Phœnicians down to our day; in short, account of stock to be taken from time to time, to know how you stand. It is a labor to tax the faculties of a man—such problems of profit and loss, of interest, of tare and tret, and gauging of all kinds, as demand a universal knowledge.

1.37.oldText: I have thought that Walden Pond would be a good place for business, not solely on account of the railroad and the ice trade; it offers advantages which it may not be good policy to divulge; it is a good port and a good foundation. No Neva marshes to be filled, though everywhere you must build on piles of your own driving. It is said that a flood tide, with a westerly wind and ice in the Neva, would sweep St. Petersburg from the face of the earth.

1.38.oldText: As this business was to be entered into without the usual capital, it may not be easy to guess where those means—still indispensable to every such undertaking—were to be obtained. As for Clothing, to come at once to the practical part of the question, perhaps we are led more often by the love of novelty, and a regard for the opinions of men, in procuring it, than by true utility. Let him who has work to do remember that the object of clothing is, first, to retain the vital heat, and secondly, in this state of society, to cover nakedness; and he may judge how much necessary or important work can be accomplished without adding to his wardrobe. Kings and queens who wear a suit only once, though made by some tailor or dressmaker to their majesties, cannot know the comfort of wearing a suit that fits. They are no better than wooden horses to hang the clean clothes on. Every day our garments become more assimilated to ourselves, receiving the impress of the wearer's character, until we hesitate to lay them aside, with such delay and medical appliances and such solemnity even as we treat our bodies. No man ever stood any lower in my estimation for having a patch in his clothes; yet I am sure that there is generally greater anxiety to have fashionable, or at least clean and unpatched, clothes than to have a sound conscience. But even if the rent is not mended, perhaps the worst vice betrayed is improvidence. I sometimes test my acquaintances by such questions as this: Who could wear a patch, or two extra seams only, over the knee? Most behave as if they believed their prospects for life would be ruined if they did it. It would be easier for them to hobble to town with a broken leg than with a broken pant-leg. Often if an accident happens to a gentleman's legs, they can be mended; but if a similar accident happens to the legs of his pantaloons, there is no help for it; for he considers, not what is truly respectable, but what is respected. We know but few men, a great many coats and breeches. Dress a scarecrow in your last shift, you standing shiftless beside it—who would not soonest salute the scarecrow? Passing a cornfield the other day, close by a hat and coat on a stake, I recognized the owner of the farm. He was only a little more weather-beaten than when I last saw him. I have heard of a dog that barked at every stranger who approached his master's premises with clothes on, but was easily quieted by a naked thief. It is an interesting question how far men would retain their relative rank if they were stripped of their clothes. Could you, in such a case, tell surely of any company of civilized men which belonged to the most respected class? When Madam Pfeiffer, in her adventurous travels round the world from east to west, had got so near home as Asiatic Russia, she says that she felt the necessity of wearing something other than a traveling dress when she went to meet the authorities, for she “was now in a civilized country, where —— — people are judged of by their clothes.” Even in our democratic New England towns, the accidental possession of wealth, and its manifestation in dress and equipage alone, obtain for the possessor almost universal respect. But those who yield such respect, numerous as they are, are so far heathen, and need to have a missionary sent to them. Besides, clothes introduced sewing—a kind of work you may call endless; a woman's dress, at least, is never done.

1.39.oldText: A man who has at last found something to do will not need to get a new suit to do it in; for him the old one will do, that has lain dusty in the garret for some indeterminate period. Old shoes will serve a hero longer than they have served his valet—if a hero ever has a valet—bare feet are older than shoes, and he can make them do. Only they who go to soirées and legislative halls must have new coats—coats to change as often as the man changes in them. But if my jacket and trousers, my hat and shoes, are fit to worship God in, they will do; will they not? Who ever saw his old clothes—his old coat, actually worn out, dissolved into its primitive elements—so that it was not an act of charity to bestow it on some poor boy, by him perchance to be bestowed on some poorer still, or shall we say richer, who could do with less? I say, beware of all enterprises that require new clothes, and not rather a new wearer of clothes. If there is not a new man, how can the new clothes be made to fit? If you have any enterprise before you, try it in your old clothes. All men want, not something to _do with_, but something to _do_, or rather something to _be_. Perhaps we should never procure a new suit, however ragged or dirty the old, until we have so conducted ourselves, so undertaken or sailed in some way, that we feel like new men in the old, and that to retain it would be like keeping new wine in old bottles. Our molting season, like that of the fowls, must be a crisis in our lives. The loon retires to solitary ponds to spend it. So also the snake casts its slough, and the caterpillar its wormy coat, by an internal industry and expansion; for clothes are but our outermost cuticle and mortal coil. Otherwise we shall be found sailing under false colors, and be inevitably cashiered at last by our own opinion, as well as that of mankind.

1.40.oldText: We don garment after garment, as if we grew like exogenous plants by addition from without. Our outside, and often thin and fanciful, clothes are our epidermis, or false skin, which does not partake of our life and may be stripped off here and there without fatal injury; our thicker garments, constantly worn, are our cellular integument, or cortex; but our shirts are our liber, or true bark, which cannot be removed without girdling and so destroying the man. I believe that all races at some seasons wear something equivalent to the shirt. It is desirable that a man be clad so simply that he can lay his hands on himself in the dark, and that he live in all respects so compactly and preparedly that, if an enemy take the town, he can, like the old philosopher, walk out the gate empty-handed without anxiety. While one thick garment is, for most purposes, as good as three thin ones, and cheap clothing can be obtained at prices really to suit customers; while a thick coat can be bought for five dollars, which will last as many years, thick pantaloons for two dollars, cowhide boots for a dollar and a half a pair, a summer hat for a quarter of a dollar, and a winter cap for sixty-two and a half cents, or a better one made at home at a nominal cost—where is the man so poor that, clad in such a suit of _his own earning_, there will not be found wise men to do him reverence?

1.41.oldText: When I ask for a garment of a particular form, my tailoress gravely tells me, “They do not make them so now,” without emphasizing the “They” at all, as if she quoted an authority as impersonal as the Fates, and I find it difficult to get made what I want, simply because she cannot believe that I mean what I say, that I am so rash. When I hear this oracular sentence, I am for a moment absorbed in thought, emphasizing to myself each word separately, that I may come at the meaning of it, that I may find out by what degree of consanguinity _They_ are related to _me_, and what authority they may have in an affair which affects me so nearly; and, finally, I am inclined to answer her with equal mystery, and without any more emphasis of the “they”—“It is true, they did not make them so recently, but they do now.” Of what use is this measuring of me if she does not measure my character, but only the breadth of my shoulders, as if I were a peg to hang the coat on? We worship not the Graces, nor the Parcæ, but Fashion. She spins and weaves and cuts with full authority. The head monkey in Paris puts on a traveler's cap, and all the monkeys in America do the same. I sometimes despair of getting anything quite simple and honest done in this world with the help of men. They would have to be passed through a powerful press first, to squeeze their old notions out of them, so that they would not soon get on their legs again; and then there would be someone in the company with a maggot in his head, hatched from an egg deposited there nobody knows when, for not even fire kills these things, and you would have lost your labor. Nevertheless, we will not forget that some Egyptian wheat was handed down to us by a mummy.

1.42.oldText: On the whole, I think it cannot be maintained that dressing has in this country, or any country, risen to the dignity of an art. At present men make shift to wear what they can get. Like shipwrecked sailors, they put on what they can find on the beach, and at a little distance, whether of space or time, laugh at each other's masquerade. Every generation laughs at the old fashions, but follows religiously the new. We are amused at beholding the costume of Henry VIII., or Queen Elizabeth, as much as if it were that of the King and Queen of the Cannibal Islands. All costume off a man is pitiful or grotesque. It is only the serious eye peering from it, and the sincere life passed within it, that restrain laughter and consecrate the costume of any people. Let Harlequin be taken with a fit of colic and his trappings will have to serve that mood too. When the soldier is hit by a cannon ball, rags are as becoming as purple.

1.43.oldText: The childish and savage taste of men and women for new patterns keeps how many shaking and squinting through kaleidoscopes that they may discover the particular figure which this generation requires today. The manufacturers have learned that this taste is merely whimsical. Of two patterns which differ only by a few threads more or less of a particular color, one will be sold readily, the other lie on the shelf, though it frequently happens that after the lapse of a season the latter becomes the most fashionable. Comparatively, tattooing is not the hideous custom it is called. It is not barbarous merely because the printing is skin-deep and unalterable.

1.44.oldText: I cannot believe that our factory system is the best mode by which men may get clothing. The condition of the operatives is becoming every day more like that of the English; and it cannot be wondered at, since, as far as I have heard or observed, the principal object is, not that mankind may be well and honestly clad, but, unquestionably, that corporations may be enriched. In the long run, men hit only what they aim at. Therefore, though they should fail immediately, they had better aim at something high.

1.45.oldText: As for a Shelter, I will not deny that this is now a necessary of life, though there are instances of men having done without it for long periods in colder countries than this. Samuel Laing says that “the Laplander in his skin dress, and in a skin bag which he puts over his head and shoulders, will sleep night after night on the snow—in a degree of cold which would extinguish the life of one exposed to it in any woollen clothing.” He had seen them asleep like that. Yet he adds, “They are not hardier than other people.” But probably man did not live long on the earth without discovering the convenience of a house, the domestic comforts—a phrase which may have originally signified the satisfactions of the house more than of the family, though these must be extremely partial and occasional in those climates where the house is associated in our thoughts chiefly with winter or the rainy season, and for two thirds of the year, except as a parasol, is unnecessary. In our climate, in summer, it was formerly almost solely a covering at night. In the Indian gazettes a wigwam was the symbol of a day's march, and a row of them cut or painted on the bark of a tree signified that they had camped that many times. Man was not made so large-limbed and robust that he must not seek to narrow his world, and wall in a space such as fitted him. He was at first bare and out of doors; but though this was pleasant enough in serene and warm weather, by daylight, the rainy season and the winter, to say nothing of the torrid sun, would perhaps have nipped his race in the bud if he had not hastened to clothe himself with the shelter of a house. Adam and Eve, according to the fable, wore the bower before other clothes. Man wanted a home, a place of warmth, or comfort—first of physical warmth, then the warmth of the affections.

1.46.oldText: We may imagine a time when, in the infancy of the human race, some enterprising mortal crept into a hollow in a rock for shelter. Every child begins the world again, to some extent, and loves to stay outdoors, even in wet and cold. It plays house, as well as horse, having an instinct for it. Who does not remember the interest with which, when young, he looked at shelving rocks, or any approach to a cave? It was the natural yearning of that portion of our most primitive ancestor which still survives in us. From the cave we have advanced to roofs of palm leaves, of bark and boughs, of linen woven and stretched, of grass and straw, of boards and shingles, of stones and tiles. At last, we no longer know what it is to live in the open air, and our lives are domestic in more senses than we think. From the hearth to the field is a great distance. It would be well, perhaps, if we were to spend more of our days and nights without any obstruction between us and the celestial bodies, if the poet did not speak so much from under a roof, or the saint dwell there so long. Birds do not sing in caves, nor do doves cherish their innocence in dovecots.

1.47.oldText: However, if one designs to construct a dwelling house, it behooves him to exercise a little Yankee shrewdness, lest after all he find himself in a workhouse, a labyrinth without a clue, a museum, an almshouse, a prison, or a splendid mausoleum instead. Consider first how slight a shelter is absolutely necessary. I have seen Penobscot Indians, in this town, living in tents of thin cotton cloth, while the snow was nearly a foot deep around them, and I thought that they would be glad to have it deeper, to keep out the wind. Formerly, when how to get my living honestly, with freedom left for my proper pursuits, was a question that vexed me even more than it does now—for unfortunately I have become somewhat callous—I used to see a large box by the railroad, six feet long by three wide, in which the laborers locked up their tools at night, and it suggested to me that every man who was hard pushed might get such a one for a dollar, and, having bored a few auger holes in it to admit the air at least, get into it when it rained and at night, and hook down the lid, and so have freedom in his love, and in his soul be free. This did not appear the worst, nor by any means a despicable alternative. You could sit up as late as you pleased, and, whenever you got up, go abroad without any landlord or house-lord dogging you for rent. Many a man is harassed to death to pay the rent of a larger and more luxurious box who would not have frozen to death in such a box as this. I am far from jesting. Economy is a subject which admits of being treated with levity, but it cannot so be disposed of. A comfortable house for a rude and hardy race, that lived mostly out of doors, was once made here almost entirely of such materials as Nature furnished ready to their hands. Gookin, who was superintendent of the Indians subject to the Massachusetts Colony, writing in 1674, says, “The best of their houses are covered very neatly, tight and warm, with barks of trees, slipped from their bodies at those seasons when the sap is up, and made into great flakes, with pressure of weighty timber, when they are green.... The meaner sort are covered with mats which they make of a kind of bulrush, and are also indifferently tight and warm, but not so good as the former.... Some I have seen, sixty or a hundred feet long and thirty feet broad.... I have often lodged in their wigwams, and found them as warm as the best English houses.” He adds that they were commonly carpeted and lined within with well-wrought embroidered mats, and were furnished with various utensils. The Indians had advanced so far as to regulate the effect of the wind by a mat suspended over the hole in the roof and moved by a string. Such a lodge was in the first instance constructed in a day or two at most, and taken down and put up in a few hours; and every family owned one, or its apartment in one.

1.48.oldText: In the savage state every family owns a shelter as good as the best, and sufficient for its coarser and simpler wants; but I think I speak within bounds when I say that, though the birds of the air have their nests, and the foxes their holes, and the savages their wigwams, in modern civilized society not more than half the families own a shelter. In the large towns and cities, where civilization especially prevails, the number of those who own a shelter is a very small fraction of the whole. The rest pay an annual tax for this outermost garment of all, which has become indispensable summer and winter, and which would buy a village of Indian wigwams, but now helps to keep them poor as long as they live. I do not mean to insist here on the disadvantage of hiring compared with owning, but it is evident that the savage owns his shelter because it costs so little, while the civilized man hires his commonly because he cannot afford to own it; nor can he, in the long run, any better afford to hire. But, answers one, by merely paying this tax the poor civilized man secures an abode which is a palace compared with the savage's. An annual rent of from twenty-five to a hundred dollars (these are the country rates) entitles him to the benefit of the improvements of centuries: spacious apartments, clean paint and paper, Rumford fireplace, back plastering, Venetian blinds, copper pump, spring lock, a commodious cellar, and many other things. But how does it happen that he who is said to enjoy these things is so commonly a _poor_ civilized man, while the savage, who has them not, is rich as a savage? If it is asserted that civilization is a real advance in the condition of man—and I think that it is, though only the wise improve their advantages—it must be shown that it has produced better dwellings without making them more costly; and the cost of a thing is the amount of what I will call life which is required to be exchanged for it, immediately or in the long run. An average house in this neighborhood costs perhaps eight hundred dollars, and to lay up this sum will take from ten to fifteen years of the laborer's life, even if he is not encumbered with a family—estimating the pecuniary value of every man's labor at one dollar a day, for if some receive more, others receive less; so that he must have spent more than half his life commonly before _his_ wigwam will be earned. If we suppose him to pay a rent instead, this is but a doubtful choice of evils. Would the savage have been wise to exchange his wigwam for a palace on these terms?

1.49.oldText: It may be guessed that I reduce almost the whole advantage of holding this superfluous property as a fund stored against the future, so far as the individual is concerned, mainly to the defraying of funeral expenses. But perhaps a man is not required to bury himself. Nevertheless, this points to an important distinction between the civilized man and the savage; and, no doubt, they have designs on us for our benefit, in making the life of a civilized people an _institution_, in which the life of the individual is to a great extent absorbed, in order to preserve and perfect the life of the race. But I wish to show at what a sacrifice this advantage is at present obtained, and to suggest that we may possibly live so as to secure all the advantage without suffering any of the disadvantage. What do you mean by saying that the poor ye have always with you, or that the fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the children's teeth are set on edge?

1.50.oldText: “As I live, saith the Lord God, ye shall not have occasion any more to use this proverb in Israel.”

1.51.oldText: “Behold all souls are mine; as the soul of the father, so also the soul of the son is mine: the soul that sinneth, it shall die.”

1.52.oldText: When I consider my neighbors, the farmers of Concord, who are at least as well off as the other classes, I find that for the most part they have been toiling twenty, thirty, or forty years, that they may become the real owners of their farms, which commonly they have inherited with encumbrances, or else bought with hired money—and we may regard one third of that toil as the cost of their houses—but commonly they have not paid for them yet. It is true, the encumbrances sometimes outweigh the value of the farm, so that the farm itself becomes one great encumbrance, and still a man is found to inherit it, being well acquainted with it, as he says. On applying to the assessors, I am surprised to learn that they cannot at once name a dozen in the town who own their farms free and clear. If you would know the history of these homesteads, inquire at the bank where they are mortgaged. The man who has actually paid for his farm with labor on it is so rare that every neighbor can point to him. I doubt if there are three such men in Concord. What has been said of the merchants—that a very large majority, even ninety-seven in a hundred, are sure to fail—is equally true of the farmers. With regard to the merchants, however, one of them says pertinently that a great part of their failures are not genuine pecuniary failures, but merely failures to fulfill their engagements, because it is inconvenient; that is, it is the moral character that breaks down. But this puts an infinitely worse face on the matter, and suggests, besides, that probably not even the other three succeed in saving their souls, but are perchance bankrupt in a worse sense than those who fail honestly. Bankruptcy and repudiation are the springboards from which much of our civilization vaults and turns its somersaults, but the savage stands on the unelastic plank of famine. Yet the Middlesex Cattle Show goes off here with _éclat_ annually, as if all the joints of the agricultural machine were running smoothly.

1.53.oldText: The farmer is trying to solve the problem of a livelihood by a formula more complicated than the problem itself. To get his shoestrings he speculates in herds of cattle.
